target.title: Learning Individual Speaking Styles for Accurate Lip to Speech Synthesis
target.version: CVPR 2020 proceedings paper (CVF Open Access PDF); first public as arXiv 2005.08209v1, submitted 2020-05-17, same text and numbers (wiki folders cvf-prajwal20-lip2wav and arxiv-2005.08209)

read.pdf: Fig. 1-5 captions and Tables 1-10 read in the full text extraction; references read

entries.text: Defines lip-to-speech synthesis as generating natural speech using only a speaker's lip movements.
entries.condition: Input is silent lip video; output is natural speech.

entries.text: Claims to study individual-speaker lip-to-speech mappings in unconstrained, large-vocabulary settings for the first time.
entries.condition: Single-speaker models; unconstrained speech and large vocabulary.

entries.text: Claims the released dataset is the first large-scale benchmark tailored to natural single-speaker lip-to-speech training and evaluation.
entries.condition: Dataset resource claim for natural settings.

entries.text: Claims its sequence-to-sequence approach is the first accurate speech-generation approach for silent lip video in unconstrained settings.
entries.condition: Lip-only input; unconstrained setting.

entries.text: Headline superiority claim: fourfold intelligibility over prior lip-to-speech works.
entries.condition: Abstract does not specify the metric aggregation; detailed unconstrained comparison is Table 4 on five single-speaker test splits against GAN-based [36] and Ephrat et al. [9].

entries.text: Authors state that only 25-30% of English is discernible from lip-reading alone.
entries.condition: Background statement about lip-reading alone, not a result of this system.

entries.text: Authors identify homophenes as a central ambiguity: distinct phonemes can have nearly identical lip shapes.
entries.condition: Intrinsic ambiguity of lip-only inference.

entries.text: Lip2Wav dataset contains about 120 hours across five speakers.
entries.condition: Talking-face videos from online lecture series and chess-analysis videos; English only.

entries.text: Each dataset speaker contributes about 20 hours and has vocabulary exceeding 5,000 words.
entries.unit: hours per speaker; words per speaker
entries.condition: Natural YouTube speech; English.
entries.quote: Each speaker has about 20 hours of YouTube video content spanning a rich vocabulary of 5000+ words

entries.text: Authors claim 800 times more data per speaker than current multi-speaker datasets.
entries.condition: Relative comparison against current multi-speaker datasets; comparator and calculation are not given.

entries.text: Contribution statement says each speaker has 80 times more data than counterparts.
entries.condition: Contribution statement; counterpart dataset is not specified there.
entries.quote: Each speaker contains 80× more data with 100× larger vocabulary than its counterparts.

entries.text: Contribution statement says each speaker has 100 times larger vocabulary than counterparts.
entries.condition: Contribution statement; counterpart dataset is not specified there.

entries.text: Table 1 reports the GRID benchmark as 34 speakers, 28 hours, 0.8 hours per speaker, and 56 vocabulary tokens, not a natural setting.
entries.unit: speakers; hours; hours/speaker; vocabulary tokens; natural-setting flag
entries.condition: Table 1 dataset comparison.

entries.text: Table 1 reports TCD-TIMIT as three speakers, 1.5 hours total, 0.5 hours per speaker, and vocabulary 82, not a natural setting.
entries.unit: speakers; hours; hours/speaker; vocabulary tokens; natural-setting flag
entries.condition: Table 1 dataset comparison.

entries.text: Table 1 reports Lip2Wav as five speakers, 120 hours, approximately 20 hours per speaker, and approximately 5,000 vocabulary items in a natural setting.
entries.unit: speakers; hours; hours/speaker; vocabulary words/speaker; natural-setting flag
entries.condition: Vocabulary count includes words occurring at least five times in the dataset.
entries.quote: Lip2Wav (Ours) 5 120 ≈20 ≈5K ✓

entries.text: Authors contrast the benchmark with multi-speaker datasets that have only about 2-5 minutes per speaker.
entries.condition: Datasets LRS2, LRW, and LRS3 are discussed in Sec. 3; statement is approximate.

entries.text: Vocabulary counts include words with frequency greater than four (equivalent to at least five occurrences).
entries.condition: Applies to the Table 1 vocabulary calculation.

entries.text: Lip2Wav is a jointly trained end-to-end sequence-to-sequence system with a spatio-temporal face encoder and attention-based speech decoder.
entries.condition: Modified Tacotron 2; face sequences condition the decoder instead of text.
entries.quote: Lip2Wav, as shown in Figure 3 consists of two modules: (i) Spatio-temporal face encoder (ii) Attention-based speech decoder.

entries.text: Mel representation uses 80 channels, 16 kHz audio, 800-sample window and 200-sample hop.
entries.condition: Audio sample rate and mel-spectrogram extraction settings.

entries.text: Visual input is a time sequence of face images encoded by 3D convolutions into one D-dimensional feature per input frame; residual skips and batch normalization are used.
entries.condition: Input tensor has dimensions T × H × W × 3; temporal dimension is preserved through the encoder.

entries.text: Training pairs a short face-video sequence with the corresponding ground-truth audio mel spectrogram; no manual text labels are required for the task.
entries.condition: Ground-truth signal is the mel spectrogram corresponding to the video segment.

entries.text: Unless otherwise stated, datasets are split 90/5/5 into train, validation, and unseen test; Lip2Wav splits use different videos and prevent any same video part from appearing in train and test.
entries.condition: Video-disjointness is explicitly stated for train versus test; speaker identities are not held out for the individual-speaker task.
entries.quote: 90-5-5% train, validation and unseen test splits

entries.text: Each training example samples a contiguous three-second video window, represented by 75 or 90 frames depending on source frame rate.
entries.condition: Random contiguous sequence; T=75 or T=90 depending on FPS.

entries.text: Video faces are detected and cropped with S3FD and resized to 48×48 for the paper's described experiments.
entries.condition: S3FD face detector; the paper states a common crop size.

entries.text: Training batch size is 32; training continues until mel reconstruction loss plateaus for at least 30,000 iterations; unconstrained single-speaker training converges at about 200,000 iterations.
entries.condition: The 200K convergence statement is for unconstrained single-speaker experiments.

entries.text: Adam optimizer uses an initial learning rate of 10^-3.
entries.condition: Model training; no scheduler-specific selection criterion reported here.

entries.text: The paper says the checkpoint with best validation-set performance is selected for testing, but does not define the selection metric.
entries.condition: Validation set is nominally 5% under the general split; metric and checkpoint-selection frequency are not given.

entries.text: Teacher forcing is used in early training up to approximately 30K iterations, then gradually decayed; the default configuration decays toward zero.
entries.condition: Ablation on Hardware Security unseen test set; gradual decay versus always forced.

entries.text: The visual context window is three seconds, stated as about six times larger than prior works using 0.3-0.5 seconds.
entries.unit: seconds; × prior context; seconds prior context
entries.condition: Longer context is intended to disambiguate homophenes; max window limited by memory.

entries.text: At inference, the system receives only lip movements, generates mel frames autoregressively, and concatenates consecutive windows with a small overlap; waveform reconstruction uses Griffin-Lim.
entries.condition: Can process arbitrary input length by independently synthesizing consecutive T-second windows.

entries.text: Authors report neural vocoders performed poorly because generated mel spectrograms were less accurate than those in state-of-the-art TTS systems; they use Griffin-Lim instead.
entries.condition: Authors' stated rationale for waveform reconstruction choice.

entries.text: Objective evaluation uses STOI and ESTOI for intelligibility, PESQ for quality, and WER after Google Speech-to-Text API recognition on GRID and TCD-TIMIT.
entries.condition: WER is not calculated for Lip2Wav because reference transcripts are unavailable.
entries.quote: We compare our models with the previous lip to speech works using three standard speech quality metrics

entries.text: WER is not reported for Lip2Wav because the corpus lacks text transcripts.
entries.condition: This applies to the proposed Lip2Wav dataset; WER is reported for GRID, TCD-TIMIT, and LRW experiments.

entries.text: Authors state Lip2Wav outperforms competitors by a significant margin across all objective metrics on GRID and TCD-TIMIT, especially on TCD-TIMIT's novel test words.
entries.condition: Constrained-dataset comparison in Tables 2 and 3.

entries.text: Authors say Lip2Wav skips words three times less often than competing methods; Table 5 reports 8.6% skips versus 24.3% and 27.5%.
entries.condition: Objective human evaluation on 50 files from the five-speaker unseen test sets; source comparator values vary.

entries.text: Authors claim the manually-transcribed-text-plus-TTS comparator cannot reproduce target-speaker prosody and naturalness, even with accurate text; they also say lips and audio can become unsynchronized.
entries.condition: Subjective evaluation includes MTT+TTS and overlays generated audio on face video.

entries.text: Encoder activations are claimed to be highly attentive to the mouth region; decoder alignment is shown to condition on corresponding lip movements.
entries.condition: Qualitative visualization on the model; figures show encoder activations and decoder alignment.

entries.text: Authors claim gradual teacher-forcing decay improves generalization to unseen vocabulary and reduces overfitting to the training vocabulary.
entries.condition: Ablation uses Hardware Security unseen test set.

entries.text: Authors report 3D-CNN is superior to the tested 2D-CNN and 2D-CNN+1D-CNN visual encoders.
entries.condition: Hardware Security unseen test predictions; decoder fixed across encoder ablation.

entries.text: Authors characterize Lip2Wav as currently the best method for natural speech generation from lip movements.
entries.condition: Claim follows objective and subjective comparisons; not a universal benchmark claim.

entries.text: Authors acknowledge speech quality and intelligibility metrics are imperfect measures, motivating human evaluation.
entries.condition: Motivation for objective human evaluation.

entries.text: Homophene errors remain a dominant source of errors in all evaluated methods, leaving room for improvement.
entries.condition: Authors' interpretation of objective human evaluation.
entries.quote: the issue of homophenes is still a dominant cause for errors in all cases indicating there is still scope for improvement in this area.

entries.text: Authors say multi-speaker lip-to-speech for random identities is highly challenging and keep the paper's main focus on single-speaker synthesis.
entries.condition: LRW experiment is word-level multi-speaker baseline only.

entries.text: The authors say the clean LRS2 training set contains only 29 hours, considered too small for multi-speaker speech generation in their comparison.
entries.condition: LRS2 clean training set, as discussed for why they do not evaluate on LRS2.

entries.text: Authors say a manually transcribed lip-to-text output followed by TTS loses prosody/naturalness and can desynchronize lips and audio.
entries.condition: Comparison uses manually transcribed text and multi-speaker TTS.

entries.text: The article does not state the number of independent training runs, seed repetitions, or uncertainty intervals for reported scores.
entries.condition: Applies across result tables and reported human/objective means.

entries.text: Released training code sets TensorFlow graph seed 5339; it defines a data random-state value 1234 but the feeder uses NumPy random sampling/shuffling without seeding NumPy, so example order is not fixed by that declaration.
entries.condition: Code behavior; paper does not report random seeds or repeat runs.

entries.text: Speaker identity overlap across train/validation/test is not reported for GRID, TCD-TIMIT, or LRW; Lip2Wav is an intentional within-speaker, video-disjoint evaluation rather than speaker-held-out evaluation.
entries.condition: Paper states video-disjoint train/test videos for Lip2Wav but not speaker overlap protocols for the other corpora.

entries.text: The validation set is named as the checkpoint-selection data, but the paper does not specify the validation metric, selection rule, or checkpoint frequency.
entries.condition: Selection data are validation; selection criterion remains unspecified.

entries.text: The public training entrypoint loads train and validation video lists, but its evaluation branch is a pass and the validation loop is commented out; this code version does not implement the paper's stated validation-based checkpoint selection criterion.
entries.condition: Code's train.py loads train/val; synthesizer/train.py saves periodic checkpoints and has no active validation metric computation.

entries.text: Paper does not report audio amplitude rescaling or mel normalization ranges; it reports STFT/mel dimensions but not those normalization operations.
entries.condition: Normalization of input waveforms, mel targets, and score-time audio is unspecified in paper text.

entries.text: Repository defaults rescale audio to maximum amplitude 0.9 and enable symmetric mel normalization clipped/scaled to max absolute value 4; presets inherit these defaults.
entries.unit: waveform max amplitude; mel max-absolute normalization
entries.condition: Defaults in synthesizer/hparams.py; speaker presets do not override these normalization values.

entries.text: The released video-ID lists contain train/validation/test counts by speaker: chem 313/17/16, chess 204/1/4, dl 113/2/2, hs 57/2/2, eh 32/1/2; these counts are not stated in the paper and vary from exact 90/5/5 proportions by ID count.
entries.condition: Released YouTube video-ID list counts; the paper may define split proportions by duration rather than number of IDs.

entries.text: The abstract's four-times intelligibility factor is not operationally defined by metric, aggregation across speakers, or comparator in the abstract.

entries.text: Authors state that Ephrat et al. [9] and the GAN-based work [36] do not use the sequence-to-sequence paradigm.

entries.quote: Previous works, however, use only about 0.3 -0.5 seconds of context. In this work, we use close to 6× this number and provide a context of 3 seconds.

entries.text: Table 4 caption claims almost 4x more intelligible speech than previous methods in unconstrained single-speaker settings.

entries.text: Authors claim to be first to study lip-to-speech in a large-vocabulary setting.
entries.quote: We are the ﬁrst to study this problem in a large vocabulary setting with thousands of words and sentences.

entries.text: For GRID and TIMIT the hidden dimension is halved to prevent overfitting.
Authors note Table 7 word-level speech metrics cannot be directly compared with the single-speaker case.
LipSound predicts mel spectrograms from mouth video with an attention encoder-decoder (Tacotron2-inspired).
entries.quote: an encoder-decoder architec- ture with attention mechanism to predict mel-spectrogram from videos

entries.text: LipSound input: whole 3-s GRID videos, 75 frames.
entries.quote: All videos are 3 seconds long and with a frame rate of 25fps (total 75 frames).

entries.text: LipSound mel generator is inspired by Tacotron2 and uses location-sensitive attention.
entries.quote: The mel-spectrogram generator is inspired by the Tacotron2

entries.text: LipSound trains its decoder with teacher forcing.
entries.quote: we use teacher-forcing training strat- egy [26] to utilize the ground truth speech spectrogram as in- put

entries.text: LipSound converts generated mel spectrograms to waveform with Griffin-Lim (50 iterations).
entries.quote: We transform the generated mel-spectrogram back to wave- form using Grifﬁn Lim algorithm [35] with 50 iterations.

entries.text: LipSound evaluation is speaker-dependent on GRID.
Vougioukas et al. feed a 7-frame window to a 3D-CNN encoder followed by a GRU.
entries.quote: We use a window of N = 7 frames as input for the generator

questions.q: Do the Table 2 GRID baseline values of the target appear in the baselines' own papers?
questions.answer: GAN-based and Lip2AudSpec WERs (26.64%, 32.51%) match Vougioukas et al. Table 2 (26.6%, 32.5%, GRID-trained ASR, 4% on ground truth); their STOI values differ (0.518 and 0.446 there); Vid2Speech reports human transcription only; Ephrat et al. report per-speaker S1-S4 values.

questions.q: Did any prior lip-to-speech synthesizer use an autoregressive attention decoder or whole-utterance context?
questions.answer: LipSound (Interspeech 2019): Tacotron2-inspired encoder-decoder with location-sensitive attention on whole 3-s GRID videos, teacher forcing, Griffin-Lim; Lip2AudSpec feeds 3-s clips to CNN + LSTM.

questions.q: Which later work gives the best like-for-like result on the Lip2Wav speakers and under which conditions?
questions.answer: RobustL2S Table IV (official split, speaker-dependent): Chemistry Lectures STOI 0.583 vs 0.416; pre-trained AV-HuBERT fine-tuned on Whisper transcripts. Niu and Mak 2023: asynchrony in Lip2Wav; vanilla STOI 0.215 vs aligned 0.760 for one output.
